## Exercise 1: Test the gene table with a grouping from the species table

Open `notebooks/03-differential.qmd`. Start by reading back the per-sample table
you saved yesterday, the one with `lacto_fraction` and `community` in it. If you
did not save it, rebuild it now; the slides from Module 2 have the recipe.

### Part 1 — Predict

1. We will test 13,738 genes. If no gene were truly different between the two
   community types, how many would come out with a raw p-value below 0.05?
2. You will test at week 18 only, which is 157 samples, 37 against 120. Would
   you rather have 157 samples at one visit or 471 samples across three visits?
   Say why before you look at anything.
3. Of the genes that do come out significant, do you expect more to be higher in
   anaerobe-dominant samples or in Lactobacillus-dominant samples?

### Part 2 — Build

1. Subset both the metadata and the gene counts to `time_point == "week_18"`.
   Confirm you have 157 samples and that the column order of the count matrix
   matches the row order of the sample table. DESeq2 will not warn you about
   this and will silently give you nonsense.

2. Filter the genes. Keep a gene if it has a count of at least 10 in at least a
   quarter of the samples.

3. Run the three lines:

   ```r
   dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(counts, sample_table, ~ community)
   dds <- DESeq(dds)
   res <- results(dds, contrast = c("community", "anaerobe", "lactobacillus"))
   ```

4. How many genes have `padj < 0.05`? How many of those have an absolute
   `log2FoldChange` above 1?

5. Join `05_gene_annotation.csv` so your results carry gene symbols rather than
   Ensembl identifiers. Sort by `padj` and read the top twenty names out loud to
   your group.

6. Draw a volcano plot: `log2FoldChange` on x, `-log10(padj)` on y, coloured by
   whether the gene passed.

7. Pick the single top gene and plot its normalised counts as a boxplot by
   community. The direction of that plot must match the sign of its
   `log2FoldChange`. Check that it does.

### Part 3 — Check the agent

- Ask Pi how many genes were significant. Then ask it how many genes went into
  the test. If it cannot tell you both numbers, it does not know what it did.
- Ask it to explain the sign convention of your contrast. Then verify against
  the boxplot from step 7. Getting the direction backwards is the single most
  common error in this analysis, and it survives peer review regularly.
- Ask it for the number of genes with `pvalue < 0.05` as well as `padj < 0.05`.
  The first number should be far larger. If it is not, something is wrong.
- Ask it to run the same test on CPM-normalised counts instead of raw counts.
  It will probably do it. Look at what happens to the results and work out why
  it is wrong.

### Discussion

- Did the direction of the effect surprise you?
- What do the top genes have in common? You do not need to know the genes; read
  the names in `gene_name` and describe the pattern in plain words.
- Someone will have used all 471 samples instead of 157. What is wrong with
  that, and how wrong is it?
